Rules / Performance

SK4031 The loop looks up a key it is already holding

foreach (var key in dict.Keys) and then dict[key] in the body: the entry was already in hand and is hashed and probed for again, once per element.

CategoryPerformance
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floorC# 7.0
Since1.3

Why

Enumerating Keys walks the same entries the dictionary would have handed over whole, and then throws the value away. Every dict[key] in the body hashes the key again, probes the bucket chain again and compares again — work the enumerator already did on the way past, multiplied by the count of the dictionary. Iterating the dictionary itself and deconstructing the pair is one pass with no hashing at all. SK1033 reports the ContainsKey-then-index double lookup; this is the same waste inside a loop, which is where it is worth a warning rather than a suggestion.

Example

Instead of:

foreach (var key in totals.Keys) {
    Console.WriteLine(key + ": " + totals[key]);
}

Write:

foreach (var (key, value) in totals) {
    Console.WriteLine(key + ": " + value);
}

When it does not fire

⚠ The receiver is matched against a closed list of framework dictionaries — Dictionary, SortedDictionary, SortedList, ReadOnlyDictionary, ImmutableDictionary, ImmutableSortedDictionary and FrozenDictionary — because the rewrite depends on Keys and the dictionary enumerating the same entries in the same order, and that is a promise those types make and IDictionary<TKey, TValue> does not. A user implementation whose Keys is a sorted projection would be reordered by the fix, so it is left alone. ⚠ `ConcurrentDictionary` is excluded, and not only for tidiness: its Keys takes every lock in the table and returns a snapshot, where iterating the table itself is a live, lock-free walk — under concurrent writes the two loops genuinely see different things, so the rewrite is a change to what the program observes rather than to what it costs. SK4033 is where that receiver's costs are reported. ⚠ A body that writes `dict[key] = …` withdraws the whole finding, not just that site: the deconstructed value is a copy and assigning to it would silently stop updating the dictionary. So does a body that reassigns the dictionary variable, or passes it by reference. ⚠ The dictionary must be reached through a name path ending in a local, a parameter or a field. A property could hand back a different dictionary on the second read, and the fix leaves the indexer's receiver text in place precisely because it is not supposed to be re-evaluated. ⚠ The loop variable must be var or exactly the key type, and the fix needs a name for the value that the enclosing body does not already use; inside a set or init accessor value is taken by the implicit parameter, so a fallback name is chosen there rather than writing CS0136. ⚠ The rule is silent below C# 7.0 and where the framework's KeyValuePair<TKey, TValue> has no Deconstruct, because the fix would not compile.
